tasks.title: Apply the ABCs of heart disease
tasks.prompt: Read the heart on this PA film step by step: heart size first (cardiothoracic ratio), then A, B, C and D as the book teaches. Write what you find at each step, then compare with the checklist.

rubric.text: Heart size first: the cardiothoracic ratio on a PA film — over 50% is enlarged. The radiologist marked this cardiac silhouette as enlarged.
A — is the left atrium enlarged? Look for a straightened or convex left heart border and a double density on the right heart border.
B — is the main pulmonary artery segment big or bulbous? Draw the tangent from the left ventricular apex to the aortic knob and see whether it bulges beyond it.
C — is that segment concave (well inside the tangent)? If so, judge the aorta: ascending only, or ascending, knob and descending all prominent.
D — is it a dilated, delta-shaped heart (very large, smooth, projecting almost equally to both sides)? Think of cardiomyopathy and pericardial effusion.
Pulmonary vessels where the steps call for it: the right descending pulmonary artery, then flow from apex to base and from hilum to periphery.
Only the enlarged heart is labelled in this dataset; the A–D answers are your own reading.

tasks.explanation: The book's system asks the questions in a fixed order after judging heart size: A, is the left atrium enlarged; B, is the main pulmonary artery big; C, is it concave; D, is the heart dilated or delta-shaped. Each answer points to a group of causes and tells you whether the pulmonary vessels or the aorta help next. This film's label (from the source dataset) confirms only that the heart is enlarged.

tasks.title: The five radiographic densities
tasks.prompt: Place an arrow on one example of each density on this chest radiograph — air, fat, soft tissue or fluid, bone or calcium, and metal if any is present — then compare with the checklist.

rubric.text: Air (blackest): the trachea and the lungs.
Fat (dark grey): the soft tissues of the chest wall, axillae and shoulders — darker than muscle.
Soft tissue or fluid (light grey): the heart, the diaphragm and the muscles.
Bone or calcium (white): the ribs, clavicles and spine.
Metal (brightest white), if present: ECG leads, wires, clips or jewelry. A film without metal is normal.

tasks.explanation: A radiograph can separate only five densities. The denser a material, the more x-rays it absorbs and the whiter it looks; and an edge is visible only where two different densities meet — which is why the heart border disappears when the lung beside it fills with fluid.

tasks.title: The CT word for bright
tasks.prompt: Bone is bright on this CT. Which description uses the right word for CT?

options.why: Echogenicity is the ultrasound word.
Lucent means dark on a radiograph; bone is the opposite.
CT describes brightness as density or attenuation: bone is hyperdense.
Intensity is the MRI word (signal intensity).

tasks.explanation: Each modality has its own words because each forms the image differently: radiographs speak of opacity and lucency, CT of density or attenuation (hyperdense, hypodense), MRI of signal intensity (hyperintense, hypointense) and ultrasound of echogenicity (hyperechoic, hypoechoic, anechoic).

options.why: Density is the CT word.
Echogenicity is the ultrasound word.
Opaque is the radiograph word.
MRI brightness is signal intensity: the lesion is hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging.

tasks.explanation: MRI describes brightness as signal intensity: bright is hyperintense, dark hypointense. CT uses density (hyperdense), radiographs opacity and lucency, ultrasound echogenicity (hyperechoic). The outlined lesion is the source dataset's expert-approved mask.

tasks.title: What is bright on T1?
tasks.prompt: This is a T1-weighted MRI without fat suppression. Which tissue is the brightest?

options.why: Fat has a short T1, so it is bright on T1-weighted images without fat suppression.
Muscle is intermediate (grey) on T1.
Fluid has a long T1 and is dark on T1; it is bright on T2.
Cortical bone has almost no signal and is black on every sequence.

tasks.explanation: Only a few substances shorten T1 and look bright on T1-weighted images: fat, gadolinium contrast, some blood products (methemoglobin) and melanin. Fluid is dark on T1 and bright on T2 — the quickest way to tell the two sequences apart is to look at fat and fluid.

tasks.title: Gadolinium enhancement
tasks.prompt: This T1-weighted image was taken after gadolinium. How does the mass at the cerebellopontine angle compare with the brain?

options.why: The mass is clearly visible at the outlined level.

options.text: Brighter than the brain — it enhances
options.why: The mass takes up gadolinium, which shortens T1: it is bright on the contrast-enhanced T1.
Enhancing tissue is bright, not dark, on post-contrast T1.
Look again: the mass stands out against the brainstem and cerebellum.

tasks.explanation: Gadolinium shortens T1, so tissue that takes it up turns bright on post-contrast T1 images. In the brain, enhancement means the blood-brain barrier is absent or broken — as in extra-axial tumors such as this vestibular schwannoma, which enhances strongly. There is no pre-contrast T1 in this study; the outline is the treating team's expert contour.
